transcript:
Header: 2026-03-04 14:00 UTC | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Sasha Kim, Marco Diaz (Redwood) — Priya Nair, Caleb Ortiz, Lena Park, Tom Ward (Meridian)

[00:00] Sasha Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really quick intro I’m Sasha with Redwood, I lead the AE team for retail. Marco our SE will do most of the demo today.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Thanks Sasha, excited to see the structured output stuff — we have a lot of downstream systems that break if the schema is off so this is top of mind.
[00:14] Marco Diaz: Great, yeah we'll focus on JSON mode, schema enforcement, function calling, and how the console and Optimize module suggests batching/quantization for cost.
[00:21] Tom Ward: Quick ask — we want streaming and deterministic keys in the JSON for our ingestion pipeline, is that possible?
[00:28] Marco Diaz: Yes, we'll show streaming with partial JSON and the console's validator that re-assembles and validates as tokens stream in. There's also a strong guardrail mode that rejects outputs that don't match schema, and a soft mode that returns best-effort plus an error flag.
[00:41] Caleb Ortiz: Also curious about tool vs function calling — we use internal microservices (product catalog, pricing) and we'd prefer Redwood to call those directly if possible.
[00:49] Marco Diaz: Absolutely, Redwood supports function calling where the model returns a structured call that your shim can map to an RPC; and tool calling which can invoke external tools from the runtime — both have different security and latency profiles. We'll demo both.

[02:05] Marco Diaz: (shares screen) Ok start with a simple schema: order_extraction with fields order_id:string, items: array of {sku:string, qty:int}, total: float, currency: string. I'll paste an example prompt and show JSON mode.
[02:20] Speaker 1: — micro background noise —
[02:30] Marco Diaz: Prompt: "Extract order info from customer chat and return JSON strictly matching schema." I'm toggling guardrail=hard. You can see the console shows the schema on the right and example valid/invalid payloads.
[02:44] Marco Diaz: Running… note the streaming tokens arriving — partial JSON chunks — the console validator highlights structurally invalid segments in red as they arrive, then green once complete.
[03:05] Priya Nair: Nice, that validator would save our ingestion errors. How do you handle extra fields?
[03:12] Marco Diaz: Two modes: strict (reject if extra fields present) and permissive (accept + include _extra_fields list). You can choose per-route.
[03:22] Lena Park: From security perspective we need to ensure no PII leaks to logs; how does Redwood handle telemetry and audit logs?
[03:30] Sasha Kim: Good question. We have redaction options, configurable retention, and we can integrate with customer KMS to encrypt logs. For Private deployment we can keep control plane in the VPC, and we have SOC2 and ISO artifacts. I'll email the security pack.

[04:55] Marco Diaz: Back to function calling: here's an example where the model outputs {"function":"get_price","args":{"sku":"ABC123"}}. The SE runtime maps that to a configured RPC and returns the response back into the prompt context.
[05:10] Marco Diaz: Tool calling: we can wire external tools (e.g., inventory check) into the runtime but that requires whitelisting and IAM roles — slightly higher operational overhead but allows direct side-effects.
[05:25] Caleb Ortiz: Latency overhead on function call vs in-model response?
[05:30] Marco Diaz: Typical extra latency is 20–80ms for local RPCs on Dedicated; public hosted varies more. Optimize will suggest batching and placement (dedicated vs hosted) based on your throughput to minimize tail latency.

[07:10] Marco Diaz: Now show schema mismatch case: I force model to output price as string instead of float. With hard guardrail the runtime flags and triggers a fallback model variant or returns an error object per route config.
[07:26] Tom Ward: Fallback behavior — can you do a secondary model that’s more precise but slower?
[07:33] Marco Diaz: Exactly — policy-based routing. We often use a faster quantized model with soft guardrails, and route failures to a full-precision variant.

[09:02] Priya Nair: What about telemetry for these guardrail failures — how do we get alerted?
[09:08] Sasha Kim: The Console exposes per-route metrics: rejection rate, schema errors, and a sample set of failed payloads (optionally redacted). You can set alerts and auto-roll-back.

[11:15] Marco Diaz: Next demo: function calling with nested schemas — I'll demo a case where the model returns a call to update inventory and then returns a final structured receipt.
[11:25] Marco Diaz: (minor transcription glitch) — "we're routing to the rabbit" — meant RabbitMQ, sorry.
[11:30] Caleb Ortiz: haha, yeah RabbitMQ or our internal queue is what we'd use. For tool calling, do you support retry/backoff semantics?
[11:36] Marco Diaz: Yes, runtime supports configurable retries, circuit breaker, and idempotency keys that you can insert via templates.

[13:55] Marco Diaz: On the Optimize side, we ran a simulation with your expected QPS and prompt lengths — console recommended a quantization profile plus a 16-token pre-cache which saved ~22% cost while keeping 95th percentile latency under 300ms.
[14:12] Priya Nair: That 95th percentile is our main SLO; how stable are those recommendations?
[14:17] Marco Diaz: They come from a heuristic engine that simulates your workload using model performance profiles. We also provide A/B rollout guardrails so you can test before full rollout.

[16:40] Lena Park: For Private deployment, how does the control plane work? We need to ensure audit logs stay in our account and key material never leaves.
[16:48] Sasha Kim: Private offers a customer-managed control plane option and integrates with your KMS/HSM. Audit logs can be routed to your S3 or Splunk; we never persist keys. We'll provide the architecture doc.

[19:05] Marco Diaz: Quick note on streaming + partial JSON: some downstream consumers need strict JSON at ingest — we recommend the console reassembly endpoint or a tiny sidecar that consumes token stream and validates on the fly.
[19:20] Tom Ward: Would Redwood host that sidecar?
[19:24] Marco Diaz: We provide a reference sidecar; hosting it in your infra is recommended for data control, but we can manage it for Dedicated customers under an SLA.

[21:00] Priya Nair: Do you offer RBAC for who can change route guardrails and schemas?
[21:06] Sasha Kim: Yes, Console has RBAC tied to SSO — roles for admin, dev, ops, and security. Schema edits can be gated behind approval workflows.

[23:12] Marco Diaz: Now the trickier bit: chaining function calls where a model calls multiple services. Here's where we demo transaction-like behavior: we can simulate a two-phase commit by using idempotency keys and compensating actions orchestrated by the runtime. It's not automatic two-phase commit but a set of primitives to build that reliably.
[23:36] Caleb Ortiz: That’s promising, we have strong consistency needs for inventory updates.

[25:50] Marco Diaz: Smaller note on model hallucinations and guardrails: schema enforcement reduces downstream breakage, but semantic hallucinations (wrong sku but valid schema) still require validation against authoritative sources — you can wire a post-validate function to cross-check SKUs against your catalog before accept.
[26:10] Tom Ward: Can the runtime call our catalog synchronously as part of validation?
[26:15] Marco Diaz: Yes as a post-processing step, either as an inline RPC or asynchronous enrichment with a tick that blocks final acceptance. You decide latency vs correctness.

[29:00] Marco Diaz: Demo wrap-up: showed strict vs permissive modes, streaming validation, function calling + tool calling, fallback policies, optimize suggestions. Anything else?
[29:12] Priya Nair: A couple of product questions: 1) How do you version schemas so we can roll forward changes? 2) How does CLI / SDK look for infra automation?
[29:22] Marco Diaz: Schema versioning is first-class — you can register a new schema version, and routes can pin to a version or use semantic selectors. CLI/SDK supports schema deploys and route config as code — we have Terraform provider in beta.

[31:40] Lena Park: On compliance we need to see the encryption-at-rest and key rotation docs — plus an architecture blurb for auditors confirming that data residency will be respected.
[31:48] Sasha Kim: I'll send the security pack and a short one-page architecture for auditors.

[33:02] Tom Ward: For the pilot, what would you recommend as a minimal success criteria?
[33:08] Marco Diaz: We usually recommend: 1) end-to-end extracted JSON validity > 98% on your test set, 2) 95th percentile latency under your target (e.g., 300ms), and 3) no retained raw PII in logs or redacted per policy.

[35:20] Priya Nair: Pricing question — how does function calling affect invoice? Is RPC cost included or is it additional outbound tooling?
[35:26] Sasha Kim: Function calling itself is within inference cost, but if you use Redwood-managed external tools or private connectors that run in our infra, there could be additional charges. We'll include that in the pricing sheet.

[37:50] Marco Diaz: Live tail: I'm going to create a failing case and show how we triage. (typing) You can see the Console sample failed payload, stacktrace from the runtime, and suggested remediations — change the guardrail to permissive or update schema.
[38:12] Caleb Ortiz: Helpful. Can we get programmatic access to those failed payloads for our SRE pipeline?
[38:18] Marco Diaz: Yes, there's an export API and webhooks.

[40:05] Sasha Kim: Recap and next steps — we'll send the security pack, sample schemas from Marco, pricing and pilot SOW draft. Customer will share sample prompts and confirm pilot participants.
[40:18] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Slight note: our legal needs a data processing addendum before the pilot.
[40:24] Sasha Kim: Understood — I'll loop in contracts and include NDA/DPAs.

[42:40] Marco Diaz: Quick follow-up on telemetry: you can set per-route retention and PII redaction templates. We also have a dev-mode that returns unredacted payloads for debugging but you must enable it explicitly and it auto-expires.
[42:52] Lena Park: We'll need that for initial debug, ok.

[44:00] Tom Ward: Great session — thanks both.
[44:05] Sasha Kim: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up within 48 hours with the docs and action items.
[44:12] Priya Nair: Thanks, bye.

(Transcript ends)
